items.plain: Comes to rely on a friend
items.explain: They lean on one close friend for support, sharing shelter, underpass and library time instead of using official services.
They are finally diagnosed with suspected tuberculosis after walking into a clinic sick, and supervised treatment may begin.
They leave hospital with nowhere to live, stop treatment, and cannot restart benefits without a postal address.
They die of a worsening lung infection made worse by hunger and sleeping rough, likely under a bridge or in emergency care.
They are expected to die in 2055, aged 49, from tuberculosis that was never properly treated.
They rarely or never pick up their blood pressure pills, so their dangerously high blood pressure stays untreated.
They use their reserved shelter bed only sometimes, sleeping under a bridge with a friend when the shelter is full or unused.
They spend a lot of close time with a friend who has untreated tuberculosis symptoms, so they will probably catch it.
Their most active helper moves away for university, and their regular Sunday shelter visits stop.
They keep turning down money from family and insist they are fine, while their situation stays the same.
The long-delayed mould repair in their flat is finally done, easing their child's wheezing.
A referral to children's services is withdrawn before anyone assesses the family, and the concern is dropped.
Their debts are combined into a small weekly payment, collectors stop calling, and money stays tight but steady.
Job centre meetings fit around school hours so benefit cuts stop, though they still rely on insecure care work plus benefits.
They stay on antidepressants long term, avoiding crisis but remaining worn out from caring work and raising a child alone.
They land a care job with guaranteed hours once their child starts secondary school, and earn a bit more.
They remain in the same council flat for years, their child moves out, and dealings with housing become routine.
Their approved protest at the council building goes ahead with very few people, since a lift repair removed the main complaint.
Their attempt to set up a tenants' group fails as neighbours distrust them and fear delaying repairs, so the group breaks up.
With no work income, their tax and fine debts grow, and they start claiming benefits with job-search requirements.
They become estranged from neighbours and switch to writing personal complaints that get filed and ignored.
They pick up occasional low-paid driving or warehouse work, and their income stays low.
They visit a clinic for the first time, likely for stress or heart problems.
They accept official agency shifts with a reference from a friend, and their criminal record stays hidden from the employer.
Their cash deposits are reviewed without any charge, but it stays on file, and a friendship fades.
They return to irregular cash jobs and sleeping under a bridge, lose phone service, and become hard to track.
They move between short-term warehouse and scrap jobs, sometimes losing work when their criminal record comes up.
After a long wait they get social housing on the edge of town, living alone on a low income.
Their record check is quietly cleared, so they can begin supervised volunteering at the library if staff approve.
They complete their suspended sentence without trouble, though police still stop them regularly without charging them.
They meet their daughter and grandson again at Christmas, as long as their drug tests stay clean.
They see their daughter and grandson regularly, which becomes the main thing keeping them from relapsing.
They stop cash scrapyard work around 64 as their body gives out, and live on benefits until pension age.
They die at 70 on their housing estate, most likely from opioids.
They resume collecting antidepressants at the clinic with a neighbour's help, though they miss their booked review.
They change their will without a lawyer, probably leaving things to their child abroad and maybe a charity.
They keep losing weight on ready meals, take medication on and off, stay low, and their blood pressure goes unchecked.
They fall or collapse at home and lie there a while before being found and taken to hospital.
The neighbouring family who helped them starts drifting away and moving, leaving no one to collect medication.
After a decline or hospital stay, selling their house and moving into a care home or near their child is considered.
They are expected to die in 2055, aged 86, from gradually wasting away and declining health.
They take questions about council computer systems to outsiders, but information requests are refused and their inquiries redirected.
They formally appeal the refusal to release information, but polite non-answers slowly drain their urgency.
They look for work elsewhere, but a heavy workload and refused leave make leaving the city hard.
They remain head librarian, their questions steered into local history work, kept in place by close friendships.
They use cash, paper notes and a switched-off phone, making their life much harder to track or predict.
They die late in life of an unknown cause, since their medical records are too thin to say.
